turn_text: We have asked for and received an opportunity to talk to US Senator Pat Toomey. So he is on the line this morning. So we get about 10 minutes with him. Thank you, Senator Toomey. Thanks for checking in with us today.
Hey, good morning guys, thanks for having me.

I really do appreciate it. Well, let's start out with coronavirus. We turn to our elected leaders to give us a straight information and not necessarily comforting words if that's not in order, but to tell us what's going on. A little preamble from you about what's going on and what's happening in Washington.

Well, I guess I think about this as a battle on two parts. The first and most important one is what can we be doing to keep Americans as safe as possible and I spent most of last week and some of this week personally very actively engaged in a great deal of my staff working tremendous hours to make sure that Pennsylvania hospital systems that are capable of developing the tests for coronavirus got all of the material they needed to do so and and uh... put it that way because people may not be aware i was not aware that even the most sophisticated labs that we have in our uh... more sophisticated hospital system of which we have several they can develop their own test kits however to validate the test they actually need a sample of the rn a right part of the genetic material of the virus itself it's harmless but it is unique to the virus and so they need that from the CDC or the NIH to complete their own validation that their test kit works. We as most people know, we really had some glitches in getting the test kits out across the country and the result of that is that we haven't been doing as many tests as we should be. That is improving daily and significantly So we'll be doing far more tests, but I can't guarantee that we won't have other bottlenecks in the process of doing these tests. And that's so essential because, first of all, people need to know if they've got the virus. They need to quarantine themselves if they're healthy enough to do so. And we need to know where it is and how it's spreading and see if we can continue to contain this. Let me say another thing I think it's important because while there's a lot we don't know about this virus, increasingly there are some things we do know. And one of the most important things we know is that first of all at this moment the chances of any individual Pennsylvania contracting the virus does seem to be quite low. As of yesterday afternoon we had 23 cases in the state of almost 13 million people. Obviously that is a very small number. But we don't know how far it's spread among people who have not been tested. So that's a fact. Here's the other thing. Young people have, it seems, overwhelmingly, recovered from this. Some many have no symptoms at all. Those that have symptoms of symptoms are very mild. I'm not aware yet of any fatalities anywhere in the world for people under the age of 20 that may have changed in the last few days. This is moving quickly. Young people's immune system seems to be very capable of defeating this virus. However, those young people, if they were to contract the virus, and I mean young, including people in their 30s and even 40s, if they were to contract the virus, even though they themselves are unlikely to be badly harmed by it, they are quite capable of passing it on to others. And there are two vulnerable categories. That would be older folks. And as you go older in the 60s, 70s, 80s, as people get older, they're progressively more at risk to serious illness and even fatality from this virus. And the other category of people who are at serious risk would be anybody of any age if they have a significant health underlying health issue that pre-exists. cardiovascular problem, breathing problems, immune system, compromise, those folks could be a danger. So I think what people should be doing is following what the CDC recommends. The CDC has great deal of expertise in this kind of thing, and they are recommending sort of mostly common sense type behavior on the part of all of us. It's what I'm engaging in. keep a little distance between you and strangers because we have no idea who's infected. Everybody should be really careful about sneezing and coughing, make sure that they're doing so discreetly and capturing it and getting into their inside of their elbow is always a good strategy. Hands should be washed as frequently as you can because this virus can survive. We don't know exactly how long, but it can survive at least briefly on hard surfaces. You know, we go through life touching doorknobs and elevator buttons and seatbelts and all kinds of things. It just makes sense to wash hands. And certainly if you are in a vulnerable category, if you're in a vulnerable category, then I think you should certainly avoid large crowds until we have a better sense of how this is playing out.
